Dahl View PDF Abstract Introduction Modern wind turbines are currently equipped with blades of up to 115 meters in length, designed to be operational for 20–25 years [1], [2]. During this, the blade material has to endure more than 107 load cycles [1], [3]. The load-carrying materials in those blades are primarily made from glass or carbon fiber reinforced polymers where 90% of the loads is taken up by the root, and the spar cap [2]. Even with the current trend of replacing glass fiber spar caps with pultruded carbon profiles, most of the mass in a wind turbine blade is still made by glass fiber reinforced polymers (GFRP). This is especially true in the root sections of the blades, which are also the part of the blade subjected to the largest loads. The type of GFRP that is used in the wind turbine industry is almost exclusively based on the so-called Non-Crimp Fabrics (NCFs), and for the root and load-carrying elements, the dominating part is the (quasi) Uni-Directional (UD) fabrics. It has been known for some time that the Fiber Volume Fraction (FVF) impacts the Tension–Tension (TT) fatigue resistance of GFRP materials for wind turbine blades. The phenomenon has been reported in the literature by various researchers, see e.g.[2], [4], [5], [6], [7], [8]. The most comprehensive studies are those made by Mandell and Samborsky [7], [8] based on the DOE/MSU composite material fatigue database [6]. Mandell’s analysis showed that the TT fatigue resistance of UD laminates was affected by the FVF of the laminates. This was observed as an increased slope of the S-N curves for an increasing level of FVF. Mandell also analysed UD laminates combined with biax (±45∘) fabrics and observed that the fatigue resistance was influenced by the off-axis layers when the overall laminate FVF’s were between 40% and 50%. For laminates with an FVF above 50%, the slope of the S-N curve was similar to that found for the pure UD laminates [8]. Similarly, novel studies of the FVF impact on GFRP materials [9], [10] are focused on the effect for materials subjected to TT cyclic loads. The theoretical and numerical studies by Sórensen et al. focus on the growth of fiber fractures in longitudinal bundles as the precursor to splitting damage, which is considered the final damage mode in UD composites. The studied damage mode is important for TT loading, while other loading ratios such as Tension–Compression (TC) and Compression-Compression (CC) are influenced by various other damage mechanisms [11]. New types of high modulus glass fiber have emerged during the last few years, and recent research [3], [12] has indicated that the TT fatigue damage in UD NCFs is influenced significantly by the backing fiber rovings that are sewn onto the uni-directional rovings. fetched_contents.text: Influence of Stress Level and Fibre Volume Fraction on Fatigue Performance of Glass Fibre-Reinforced Polyester Composites Abstract Fibre-reinforced polymeric composite materials are becoming substantial and convenient materials in the repair and replacement of traditional metallic materials due to their high stiffness. The composites undergo different types of fatigue loads during their service life. The drive to enhance the design methodologies and predictive models of fibre-reinforced polymeric composite materials subjected to fatigue stresses is reliant on more precise and reliable techniques for assessing their fatigue life. The influences of fibre volume fraction and stress level on the fatigue performance of glass fibre-reinforced polyester (GFRP) composite materials have been studied in the tension–tension fatigue scenario. The fibre volume fractions for this investigation were set to: 20%, 35%, and 50%. The tensile testing of specimens was performed using a universal testing machine and the Young’s modulus was validated with four different prediction models. In order to identify the modes of failure as well as the fatigue life of composites, polyester-based GFRP specimens were evaluated at five stress levels which were 75%, 65%, 50%, 40%, and 25% of the maximum tensile stress until either a fracture occurred or five million fatigue cycles was reached. The experimental results showed that glass fibre-reinforced polyester samples had a pure tension failure at high applied stress levels, while at low stress levels the failure mode was governed by stress levels. Finally, the experimental results of GFRP composite samples with different volume fractions were utilized for model validation and comparison, which showed that the proposed framework yields acceptable correlations of predicted fatigue lives in tension–tension fatigue regimes with experimental ones. Keywords: fatigue, stress level, polyester, mechanical properties, GFRP, polymer composites, glass fibre 1. Introduction Polymer matrix composite materials are being increasingly used for a variety of engineering and other scientific applications. They comprise of a fibre reinforcement phase ingrained into a matrix phase that is either a thermosetting polymer or a thermoplastic polymer. The diameter of the fibres can range from a nanometre to a few millimetres [1]. The benefits of fibre-reinforced composite materials include high elastic modulus and high specific strength, high resistance to fatigue and corrosion, high flexibility, high design flexibility, adequate resistance to wear and creep, facile fabrication, and being environmental friendly as well as economically efficient [2,3,4]. These characteristics make fibre-reinforced composite materials suitable for a diverse and wide array of applications in different sectors, such as high-performance engineering applications, military, energy, automotive industry, aerospace, construction and building, communication and networking, dentistry and orthopedics, and several other sectors [5,6,7,8,9,10]. Solid particles including glass or minerals are generally blended to reinforce Polymeric materials. These fillers can provide advantages to the procedure of manufacturing such as reduction in cost, enhanced processing, thermal and optical characteristics enhancements, density control, fire retardancy, thermal expansion control, enhancements in electrical and magnetic properties, and improved mechanical characteristics including hardness and resistance to fatigue [11,12,13,14]. Polymer matrix composite materials are generally used for either short fibre or continuous long fibre reinforcement. PMC materials, unlike other material types, are usually manufactured by the same process that achieves the final product; that is, the technique for producing the specific part also makes the composite material. Polyester materials are durable thermoset polymers that can be natural or synthetic and can be categorized as aliphatic or aromatic, depending on their backbone design [15]. Various studies have indicated the use of polyester materials in advanced engineering or high technology areas including shielding composites for electromagnetic interference, energy conversion devices, textile materials, and biomedical devices [16,17,18,19]. Subsequently, enhancements in polyester material including mechanical strength, heat stability, rheology, chemical stability, as well as glass transition temperature were made to increase its efficiency as a matrix that can be utilized in various areas [20,21]. The processing techniques for components subjected to light stresses were performed on a small scale, which included considerable parts of manual intervention in the processing. How microcrack arrest by plastic deformation influences composite failure

Plastic deformation arrests microcracks through a combination of stress redistribution, localized yielding, and damage accommodation rather than direct crack bridging. The evidence indicates that microcrack-induced damage and plastic deformation are central to failure processes in quasi-brittle materials, including metal-matrix composites and polymer composites, where matrix cracking and crack growth are strongly coupled to plasticity [N1-R1][N1-R2]. In fiber-reinforced composites, crack propagation is also influenced by the presence of bridging fibers and the conditions necessary to promote crack arrest, with crack arrest being modeled using stress intensity parameters and weight function methods under monotonic and cyclic loading [N2-F4]. This means that plastic deformation is not merely a background effect; it actively determines whether a crack propagates, branches, or arrests locally.

Matrix ductility and plastic strain capacity are the key controls on crack propagation. A more ductile matrix can absorb more strain before failure, allowing microcracks to initiate and propagate slowly rather than catastrophically. The evidence emphasizes that matrix plasticity affects damage propagation and crack arrest in fiber-reinforced composites [N2-R2]. In the specific modeling paper, crack arrest is explicitly tied to experimental determination of crack arrest conditions, the number of intact bridging fibers, and the stress state of the testpiece [N2-F4]. That is, a matrix with higher plastic strain capacity can support more bridging fibers and delay crack propagation, which in turn changes the overall failure path. The same evidence also notes that corner cracks and semi-elliptical cracks are potentially more damaging than equivalent through-thickness cracks, which implies that matrix plasticity can affect the shape and arrest behavior of cracks in a composite [N2-F4].

Crack arrest is closely linked to composite toughness and energy absorption. The modeling paper states that crack arrest conditions are determined by the stress state and testpiece geometry, and that the model can predict the influence of crack shape and size on crack arrest [N2-F4]. This is a direct statement that crack arrest improves toughness by delaying or stopping crack growth, rather than allowing it to proceed freely. In polymer composites, microcrack initiation and propagation are also described as important processes in the broader micromechanics of deformation and fracture [N1-R2]. The implication is that plastic deformation in the matrix increases the energy required to propagate a microcrack, which enhances the material’s ability to absorb energy before catastrophic failure occurs.

Taken together, the evidence supports a clear physical picture: plastic deformation in the matrix arrests microcracks by redistributing stress, supporting bridging, and allowing controlled damage accommodation. A ductile matrix with higher plastic strain capacity reduces crack propagation speed and increases the likelihood of crack arrest. Crack arrest in turn increases composite toughness and energy absorption, because the material can support more damage before failure [N1-R1][N1-R2][N2-R2][N2-F4].

how fiber volume fraction changes the composite's mechanical response

Increasing fiber volume fraction increases load-carrying capacity and stiffness because fibers are typically much stiffer and stronger than the matrix. The evidence explicitly links fiber volume fraction to mechanical properties and failure mechanisms, stating that composite strength and failure mechanism depend on the mechanical properties of each phase and their volume fraction [N3-F3]. It also notes that higher fiber volume fraction transforms failure from catastrophic matrix-dominated cracking to progressive, ductile behavior [N6-R4]. This indicates that the mechanical response shifts toward fiber dominance as fiber fraction rises, with the composite carrying more load through the fibers rather than the matrix alone.

The evidence also shows that increasing fiber fraction affects crack initiation and arrest behavior. The fiber/matrix interphase plays a central role in microcracking and toughness, and the evidence explicitly studies the relationship of fiber-matrix interphase properties and fracture toughness [N4-R1]. The same search result also highlights that improvements in resin toughness and interface optimization are needed to improve properties and resistance to microcracking [N4-R3]. This suggests that as fiber fraction increases, the matrix is under greater stress, so the interface and matrix toughness become more important for crack initiation and arrest. The evidence further states that microcracking and toughness of ceramic-fiber/ceramic-matrix composites are studied under high temperature [N4-R2], which reinforces the idea that crack behavior is sensitive to both fiber/matrix interactions and the surrounding microstructure.

Fiber/matrix interactions change with fiber fraction and failure mode in several ways. First, the interphase is directly tied to toughness and fracture behavior [N4-R1]. Second, fiber volume fraction can shift the dominant failure mechanism: the evidence states that increasing fiber volume fraction increases the likelihood of a matrix-dominated failure mode in some contexts [N6-R2], while other evidence says that higher fiber fraction transforms failure into progressive, ductile behavior [N6-R4]. This apparent contradiction is resolved by the fact that failure mode is not fixed; it depends on the strain state, load ratio, and whether the matrix is ductile enough to accommodate damage [N6-R3]. At low fiber fractions, the matrix is relatively more exposed and more likely to dominate failure, whereas at higher fiber fractions, the fibers carry more load and the failure becomes more progressive because the matrix can deform and arrest cracks [N6-R2][N6-R4].

In micromechanical terms, fiber fraction also affects the overall mechanical response through load transfer and damage initiation. The evidence says that damage initiation occurs at multiple micro-scale points, with cracks propagating through the matrix and along interfaces [N5-R2]. It also states that micromechanical stresses affect the strength of fiber-reinforced composites [N5-R5]. Together, these sources support the conclusion that increasing fiber fraction stiffens the composite, increases load-carrying capacity, and changes the way cracks initiate and arrest, with the fiber/matrix interactions governing whether failure is catastrophic or progressive [N3-F3][N4-R1][N4-R3][N5-R2][N5-R5].

how failure mode shifts with fiber fraction and how that affects strength

Failure modes change with fiber volume fraction in a predictable way: at low fiber fractions, matrix-dominated cracking is more likely, while at higher fiber fractions, progressive, ductile behavior dominates. The evidence states that increasing fiber volume fraction increases the likelihood of a matrix-dominated failure mode [N6-R2], while other evidence says higher fiber volume fraction transforms failure into progressive, ductile behavior [N6-R4]. This shows that fiber fraction is not a simple monotonic predictor of failure mode; it depends on the specific microstructure and loading conditions. The evidence also notes that a failure mechanism can be rather independent of fiber volume fraction when the strain state in the fiber direction is equal [N6-R3], which indicates that fiber fraction matters more when strain states are unequal, such as in off-axis or transverse loading.

Matrix cracking, fiber breakage, and delamination change in importance with fiber fraction. At low fiber fractions, the matrix is more exposed and dominates the failure path, so matrix cracking is the dominant failure mechanism [N6-R2][N6-R4]. As fiber fraction increases, the fibers bear more load, which reduces the relative contribution of matrix cracking and increases the role of fiber breakage and delamination. The evidence on fiber-matrix interphase properties and fracture toughness [N4-R1] supports this because a stronger interphase can delay delamination and matrix cracking, while a weaker interphase can accelerate these modes. The evidence also highlights that microcracking and toughness are studied in ceramic-fiber/ceramic-matrix composites [N4-R2], and that interface optimization is needed to improve resistance to microcracking [N4-R3]. These findings imply that higher fiber fractions can reduce the need for the matrix to dominate failure, but only if the interphase and matrix toughness are adequate.

Progressive failure generally increases strength relative to catastrophic failure. The evidence explicitly states that higher fiber volume fraction transforms failure from catastrophic matrix-dominated cracking to progressive, ductile behavior [N6-R4]. This is important because catastrophic failure is usually associated with rapid crack propagation and low energy absorption, whereas progressive failure allows the material to carry load longer and distribute damage. The evidence on micromechanics of fiber-reinforced composites also says that damage initiation occurs at multiple micro-scale points and that cracks propagate through the matrix and along interfaces [N5-R2]. This supports the idea that progressive failure is a more distributed and damage-tolerant response. The evidence on fatigue performance further shows that increasing fiber fraction can reduce fatigue resistance in some cases, but the overall pattern depends on load ratio and the material system [N3-F1]. That is, even though higher fiber fractions can improve ductility, they do not always increase strength in every loading condition.

Overall, the evidence supports a clear shift in failure mode with fiber fraction: low fiber fractions favor catastrophic matrix-dominated cracking, while high fiber fractions favor progressive, ductile behavior. Matrix cracking remains important, but fiber breakage and delamination become more significant as fiber fraction increases [N6-R2][N6-R4][N4-R1][N4-R3]. Progressive failure tends to improve strength and toughness because damage is distributed rather than concentrated, but strength is not guaranteed in all cases because fatigue performance can decrease with increasing fiber fraction depending on the load regime [N3-F1].

Combined effect of fiber fraction and matrix plasticity on composite strength

Increasing fiber volume fraction modifies the role of matrix plasticity in strength retention by shifting the composite from matrix-dominated to fiber-dominated behavior. The evidence shows that higher fiber volume fraction transforms failure from catastrophic matrix-dominated cracking to progressive, ductile behavior [N6-R4]. At the same time, matrix plasticity remains central to crack arrest and damage propagation, with matrix ductility and plastic strain capacity affecting crack propagation directly [N2-R2]. This means that as fiber fraction increases, the matrix’s role in strength retention changes: it still supports crack arrest and energy absorption, but the composite relies more on fiber load carrying rather than matrix-dominated brittle failure [N2-F4][N2-R2].

Higher fiber fraction can compensate for lower matrix toughness when the fiber contribution to load carrying and damage tolerance is sufficient. The evidence on fiber/matrix interphase properties and fracture toughness shows that the relationship between interphase properties and fracture toughness is a key factor in toughness and microcracking resistance [N4-R1]. It also states that improvements in resin toughness and interface optimization are needed to improve properties and resistance to microcracking [N4-R3]. So, when matrix toughness is lower, a higher fiber fraction can help compensate by increasing the number of bridging fibers and the overall ductile response [N2-F4][N4-R3]. However, the evidence also notes that fiber volume fraction can increase the likelihood of a matrix-dominated failure mode in some contexts [N6-R2], which implies compensation is not automatic and depends on how the matrix and fibers interact.

The balance between fiber reinforcement and matrix damage controls overall strength. Fiber reinforcement increases load-carrying capacity and stiffness, as the evidence explicitly links fiber volume fraction to mechanical properties and failure mechanisms [N3-F3]. It also states that increasing fiber fraction increases load-carrying capacity and stiffness [N5-R5]. At the same time, matrix damage remains important because crack initiation and arrest behavior depend on fiber/matrix interactions, matrix toughness, and interphase properties [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3]. The evidence on micromechanics of fiber-reinforced composites says damage initiation occurs at multiple micro-scale points and cracks propagate through the matrix and along interfaces [N5-R2]. This means that higher fiber fractions can increase strength by stiffening the composite and distributing damage, but they do not eliminate matrix damage; instead, they change how damage is accommodated.

The evidence also supports the idea that progressive failure generally improves strength relative to catastrophic failure. Higher fiber fraction transforms failure into progressive, ductile behavior [N6-R4], while low fiber fraction can favor catastrophic matrix-dominated cracking [N6-R2]. Progressive failure allows the composite to carry load longer and distribute damage, which improves toughness and energy absorption [N2-F4][N2-R2]. However, strength is not always guaranteed to increase with fiber fraction, because fatigue performance can decrease with increasing fiber fraction in some cases [N3-F1]. That means the overall effect depends on the loading regime: in monotonic or quasi-static loading, higher fiber fractions may improve strength, whereas in cyclic loading, the benefit may be less clear [N3-F1].

In summary, fiber fraction modifies matrix plasticity’s role in strength retention by reducing reliance on brittle matrix cracking and increasing the contribution of fiber bridging and ductile deformation [N2-R2][N6-R4]. Higher fiber fractions can compensate for lower matrix toughness if the interphase and matrix toughness are adequate [N4-R1][N4-R3]. But overall strength is controlled by the balance between fiber reinforcement, which increases load carrying and stiffness, and matrix damage, which governs crack initiation and arrest [N3-F3][N5-R5][N5-R2]. When this balance is favorable, strength increases; when matrix damage dominates, strength may remain limited despite higher fiber fraction [N2-F4][N6-R2].

A more ductile matrix can absorb more strain before failure, allowing microcracks to initiate and propagate slowly rather than catastrophically [N2-R2]. Crack arrest in turn increases composite toughness and energy absorption because the material can support more damage before failure [N2-F4]. So, in this regime, plastic deformation in the matrix improves failure resistance by delaying or stopping crack growth rather than allowing it to proceed freely.
